question: The authors single out SheetRM, a spreadsheet benchmark that explicitly aims at long-horizon tasks. Why do they still say it falls short of realistic finance work?
options: It makes tasks longer by using very large workbooks, so the agent mainly struggles to read enough of each sheet
It makes tasks longer by concatenating well-defined instructions, so the agent never has to infer the plan itself
It makes tasks longer with multi-tab models, but it builds them from public coding repositories rather than finance work
It makes tasks longer through vague prompts, but it then grades every attempt with a single overall correctness score

private.explanation: The authors say SheetRM modulates difficulty by simply concatenating relatively well-defined manipulation instructions. Realistic finance requests are underspecified, so a capable agent must infer a viable plan and meet implicit domain expectations. The tempting wrong answer is the 'vague prompts' one, because the authors do criticise benchmarks that compress evaluation into a single score, but SheetRM's instructions are explicit rather than vague.
option_explanations: The page does not describe SheetRM's difficulty as coming from workbook size or reading limits. Think about how its instructions are written.
Right. Chaining explicit, well-defined edits produces length without underspecification. Real finance requests leave the plan to the agent, along with implicit domain expectations.
The page says nothing about SheetRM drawing on code repositories. The criticism is about how its difficulty is produced.
This gets SheetRM's prompts backwards. The authors' complaint concerns how clearly its instructions are spelled out, not that they are vague.
